description:
Camille Ann Brewer lives and works in the City of Detroit, Michigan.  Through the process of textile construction, Brewer’s artwork intersects cartographic and photographic images that speak to specific spaces and time. Weaving together of physical place, memory with time is the core subject of this body of work.  

The artwork is built with time-period paper maps, which illustrate spatial geography and political territory; along with paper-collaged images of people, places and things, which tie directly to the history and human relationships in space.  In patterns that support the artwork’s theme, the two disparate paper elements are then woven together to create a serendipitous making and aesthetic experience.

combined_title: Comics Beyond Sight
description:
This exhibit covers a variety of creative approaches to comics visual accessibility, and by extension visual accessibility broadly. Those approaches range from multimedia (audio and textual descriptions) through multidimensional and emerging technologies strategies (3D printing, haptics, and screen-based mobile touch interfaces). It demonstrates that comics can be made accessible. Learn about the international efforts of innovators in the realm of comics accessibility for those who are blind or have low vision, assembled by the Accessible Comics Collective at San Francisco State University (SFSU) with the expertise of blind access professionals. 

Emily Beitiks was the accessibility lead for the content creation of the exhibit. She is the co-director for the San Francisco Disability Cultural Center (the first civically funded disability culture center on the planet!), and prior to that, the director of the Longmore Institute on Disability. 

Nick Sousanis (SFSU), the lead creative organizer of the exhibit, is a Detroit native and was the first person to draw his dissertation in comics format, subsequently published as the graphic novel Unflattening.

View the exhibit anytime the Hatcher Library is open, and join us for an opening presentation on Friday, October 2nd, 1:00pm - 4:00pm.

description:
Lila Kadaj received her MFA from Wayne State University. Her work has been shown at numerous institutions, including the Detroit Institute of Arts, the Cranbrook Art Museum, and the Arab American National Museum.  She spent nearly 27 years teaching art at Detroit Public schools.

Artist statement: “When looking at a beautiful flower.  It’s just itself.  Just there......no .....it does not proclaim its purpose for blooming is to make people happy. It just is. Like standing in front of an easel and painting........just is.......no matter......what proclamations may be concluded to sway the viewer. Same thing goes for fine art.  It’s not about I am a woman....it’s not about I am a first generation Arab American.....it’s not about being a child of trauma....it’s not about a member of my family being gunned down on the street....it’s about being born a painter.....standing in front of my easel and working to create a "Piece of Fine Art". Not standing on some soap box and expecting my words to somehow qualify my painting. It’s the painting, drawing or sculpture that must speak on its own.......on how the artist......via the intellect and muse uses the elements to create something distinct and first rate.   It can be quiet or loud. I see so much very weak work uplifted not for its quality but because it’s in fashion.”

event_title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
combined_title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
description:
Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union.

Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky  portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration.  

“For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.”
— Galina Lembersky, daughter

Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director.

Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky.

combined_title: Black Birth Joy: Announcing Lane Hall’s Fall Exhibition
description:
Black Birth Joy by Tiana Lashae documents birth as a deeply personal story of connection, courage, tenderness, and joy. The photographs and stories in the exhibit challenge mainstream narratives that reduce Black birth to statistics and only amplify Black pregnant women's anxiety and hesitancy about navigating the maternal health care system. Instead, the exhibit offers evidence of joy, reminders of possibility, and a visual legacy for generations to come. 
 
Black Birth Joy was born from Lashae's belief that more positive birth stories of BIPOC families need to be seen and heard, and her photographs invite viewers to witness the people behind them: the mothers, babies, partners, families, and birthworkers. They create space for BIPOC families to see themselves represented with dignity and to witness the full range of birth experiences. Lashae's photographs also create a tangible record that can support conversations around quality of medical care, respectful treatment, and patient rights. The exhibit empowers women to prioritize and advocate for their birth experiences while also encouraging perinatal health professionals and birthworkers to center the humanity, dignity, and individual experiences of patients and families. 

The exhibit comprises over 30 photographs as well as stories of mothers whose births were documented by Lashae, a doula and birth/newborn photographer whose work has been published in Everyday Birth Magazine, an international publication. The physical exhibit is accompanied by a virtual component that encourages audiences to engage with each mother's birth story.

The Lane Hall Exhibit Space is sponsored by the Institute for Research on Women and Gender (IRWG) and the Department of Women’s and Gender Studies (WGS) at the University of Michigan.

Visit the Hatcher Gallery Exhibit Room to see historical materials that illustrate women’s changing relationship with food, cooking, and technology during the heady decade of the 1920s, sandwiched between WWI and the Great Depression. This exhibit features materials from the Janice Bluestein Longone Culinary Archive, as well as select items from the Art, Architecture, and Engineering Special Collections and the Transportation History Collection.

As America rang in a new decade in the 1920s, cookbook authors and appliance manufacturers stood ready to offer the newly emancipated and forward-thinking American woman a vision for her future, a vision that would be scientifically  grounded, speedy enough to make time for leisure as well as housework, and guaranteed to bring fun to that most humdrum of chores: planning and preparing meals for a family three times a day, 365 days a year.

combined_title: Like the flowing river: An exhibition by Tomoyuki Ueno
description:
Artist Tomoyuki Ueno creates individual works and installations where nature appears to be in an endless conversation with form, one echoing the other, a repetition. They are a combination of certainty and ephemerality, as if hinged between living and loss. The specificity of Ueno’s sculptural works reads like poetry. Ueno’s installation offers visitors time away, for contemplation, to draw inward, to come inside, to ask the question, “How are art and the everyday intertwined?” Honoring the Buddhist philosophy of impermanence, one becomes a continuation of the other. The artist intends the space to offer a restorative and meditative experience.

This exhibition includes artworks created from natural materials foraged by the artist while in artist residency in Ann Arbor.

*The title refers to the opening line of Hōjōki, written by 13th-century Japanese Buddhist monk Kamo no Chōmei: "The flow of the river is ceaseless, and the water is never the same…"*

Small Works
Prints & Book Objects from Detroit 2020–2026

October 27 - November 19 
Public Reception: Friday, November 13 from 4:30-6pm.

Small Works was a print shop ran by Li Chen & Gerald Schulze, in Detroit, MI, from 2020–2026. Mariana Matos joined as the studio assistant, and later studio manager, in 2024. Over those six years, the business grew from an extension of their design practice to a community space that hosts more than 70 classes a year, open studio for the public, and year long funded fellowships that investigate practice in art and design related to the Book Arts. In 2026, they decided to expand community programming, and to accommodate this expansion closed Small Works, and formed Center for the Book Arts Detroit (BAD) which operates in the same space.

This exhibition is a eulogy for the former Small Works shop, and a celebration of all the people who made work here. It also serves to show what is possible as a community, when they share space and create work together. 

The work featured is a collection of things printed by Small Works, by their studiomates Diskette Press, the publisher Maamoul Press, and by the community that uses the space.

event_title: When AI Gets It Wrong: Learning Generative AI Through Its Mistakes
combined_title: When AI Gets It Wrong: Learning Generative AI Through Its Mistakes: Deep Dive into Digital and Data Methods for Chinese Studies
event_subtitle: Deep Dive into Digital and Data Methods for Chinese Studies
description:
Generative AI tools often make mistakes, especially with historical East Asian sources. This hands-on workshop, led by Kwok-leong Tang from Harvard University, uses those mistakes to explain how the technology works, so that participants can decide when to trust it and when to use it.

No technical background is needed, and you can attend in person or register to join via Zoom (https://myumi.ch/zNnZM). A laptop is required for in-person participants — the Hatcher Gallery Lab is equipped with laptops, but please feel free to bring your own.

When an AI tool gives a wrong answer, there are two possible reasons: the model itself cannot do the task, or we have not given it what it needs. The workshop teaches how to tell these apart. First, we will run a small AI model on our own laptops and look inside it: how it reads text, how it chooses each word, and why it can sound certain and still be wrong. Next, we will see how clearer instructions, more context, or a connected tool can fix some mistakes but not others. Finally, we will practice a simple way to test an AI answer: ask the same question several times and check the results against a reliable source.

Kwok-leong Tang serves as the managing director of the Digital China Initiative and a lecturer for the Department of East Asian Languages and Civilizations at Harvard University. By training, he is a historian. He received his bachelor’s and master’s degrees in history from the Chinese University of Hong Kong and a Ph.D. in history and Asian Studies from Pennsylvania State University. In recent years, he has focused on exploring the potential of new technologies in humanities research. He has organized and instructed workshops on adopting GenAI in Chinese studies and humanities research at Harvard and other institutions.

The Deep Dive into Digital and Data Methods for Chinese Studies series is sponsored by the U-M Library (Asia Library) and the Lieberthal-Rogel Center for Chinese Studies. For inquiries, please contact asialibrary@umich.edu.

event_title: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”
combined_title: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”
description:
Changes over the course of the nineteenth century in how Americans voted, from voice vote to public ballot box to private voting booth, also saw changes in the material culture that surrounded voting. Ballots and ballot boxes, campaign pins and ribbons, blank lists and pre-printed party tickets, lanterns and banners–the creative forces of the American print industry filled the country’s cities and small towns with the ephemera of electioneering.

As you look at the items in this exhibit, think about what they tell us about how Americans in the past felt about voting, and about how voting felt. How did Election Days feel when they were full of parades and music and public drinking? What was it like to vote when everyone around you knew who you voted for? And, most of all, who counted as a voter, and who did the counting?

On view September 11-December 22, weekdays from 12-4 pm.

event_title: Applied Physics | From Solar Eruptions to Radiation Forecasts: Plasma Physics with CLEAR and SOFIE
combined_title: Applied Physics | From Solar Eruptions to Radiation Forecasts: Plasma Physics with CLEAR and SOFIE: Lulu Zhao, Assistant Professor, Department of Climate and Space Sciences and Engineering, University of Michigan
event_subtitle: Lulu Zhao, Assistant Professor, Department of Climate and Space Sciences and Engineering, University of Michigan
description:
How can we predict the radiation environment in space before it threatens astronauts and spacecraft? Solar eruptions can accelerate charged particles to nearly the speed of light, creating solar energetic particle (SEP) events that pose a major challenge for space exploration. Predicting these events requires connecting processes across vastly different scales, from particle acceleration at shocks to transport through the Sun’s evolving magnetic environment.

In this talk, I will introduce the Center for All-Clear Solar Energetic Particle Forecasts (CLEAR), a NASA Space Weather Center of Excellence developing an integrated framework to predict both hazardous SEP events and periods of low radiation risk. I will focus on SOFIE, the Solar Wind with Field Lines and Energetic Particles modeling framework, which connects simulations of the solar wind, coronal mass ejections, shock acceleration, and energetic particle transport. Through examples, I will discuss how magnetic connectivity and the evolving solar-wind environment shape the particle intensities and energy spectra experienced at different locations in space. I will also explore the challenges of turning physical understanding into reliable forecasts, including limited observations, uncertain model inputs, and validation against spacecraft measurements. The talk will highlight how fundamental plasma physics and computational modeling come together to support human exploration of the Moon and Mars.

description:
Economics graduate student Austin Zhu performs on the Charles Baird Carillon, an instrument of 53 bronze bells located inside the Burton Memorial Tower. The largest bell, which strikes the hour, weighs 12 tons, while the smallest bell, 4½ octaves above, weighs just 15 pounds.

Thirty-minute recitals are performed on the Charles Baird Carillon at noon every weekday that classes are in session, followed by visitor Q&A with the carillonist. The bell chamber may be accessed via a combination of elevator and stairs. Take the elevator to the highest floor possible (floor 8), and then climb two flights of stairs (39 steps) to the bell chamber (floor 10). Hearing protection earmuffs are provided for visitors. Be prepared to walk on ice and snow in the bell chamber during winter. Built in 1936, the Charles Baird Carillon is not ADA accessible. Visitors with mobility concerns are invited to visit the Lurie Carillon.

combined_title: From Printed Page to Research Data: Building Humanities Tools with AI Agents: Deep Dive into Digital and Data Methods for Chinese Studies
event_subtitle: Deep Dive into Digital and Data Methods for Chinese Studies
description:
Attend a live demonstration, where Kwok-leong Tang, Harvard University, shows how AI coding agents, such as Claude Code, let a humanist build research tools by describing them in plain language, without being a trained programmer.

Attend in person or register to join via Zoom (https://myumi.ch/Ax23x). No laptop or setup is needed for in-person attendees.

The main demonstration is a full pipeline that turns printed materials into structured data: scanned pages go through OCR (turning page images into text), and the text then becomes a table of people, places, and dates, each checked against reference databases such as Wikidata and CBDB (China Biographical Database Project). Dr. Tang will also show other tools he has built this way, including a batch OCR tool, a converter for historical Chinese, Japanese, and Korean dates, a tool that suggests Library of Congress subject headings, and classroom history games made from primary sources. Throughout, we will look at how to check the agent's work and where this approach breaks down.

Following the demonstration, 3:45-5:00 pm, Dr. Tang will host an optional office hour for in-person participants who are interested in discussing their own projects related to AI and East Asian studies. This informal session offers an opportunity to receive feedback, explore possible approaches, and consider both the potential and limitations of AI tools for your projects.

Kwok-leong Tang serves as the managing director of the Digital China Initiative and a lecturer for the Department of East Asian Languages and Civilizations at Harvard University. By training, he is a historian. He received his bachelor’s and master’s degrees in history from the Chinese University of Hong Kong and a Ph.D. in history and Asian Studies from Pennsylvania State University. In recent years, he has focused on exploring the potential of new technologies in humanities research. He has organized and instructed workshops on adopting GenAI in Chinese studies and humanities research at Harvard and other institutions.

The Deep Dive into Digital and Data Methods for Chinese Studies series is sponsored by the U-M Library (Asia Library) and the Lieberthal-Rogel Center for Chinese Studies. For inquiries, please contact asialibrary@umich.edu.

event_title: HEP-Astro Seminar | HEP-Astro Seminar | Flavor Dependent Jet Fragmentation and Open Science at LHCb
combined_title: HEP-Astro Seminar | HEP-Astro Seminar | Flavor Dependent Jet Fragmentation and Open Science at LHCb: Dillon Fitzerald (U-M Physics)
description: One of the remaining mysteries of the Standard Model is how emergent properties of hadronic matter arise from quark and gluon degrees of freedom. For example, there is still much to be learned about the process by which hadrons are formed from color charged quarks and gluons (hadronization). The LHCb detector offers a unique opportunity to study this process in terms of the flavor of quarks involved in the hard scattering process, enabling measurements of the fragmentation process in heavy flavor jets with unprecedented precision. The unique features of these data motivate both a substantial effort to extract high precision measurements of heavy and light flavor jets, as well as an effort to preserve and provide open access to these data for the physics and data science communities to explore. In this talk, I will review recent jet fragmentation function measurements from LHCb in comparison to global measurements. I will then briefly cover the LHCb open data efforts, culminating in the review of a publicly available dataset and analysis workflow enabling exploration of the jet fragmentation process at LHCb.

event_title: Math Grad Show and Tell Seminar: A mathematical introduction to knitting
combined_title: Math Grad Show and Tell Seminar: A mathematical introduction to knitting: Veronica Lang
description:
Suppose you want a nice two-dimensional surface, but only have some one-dimensional string. Is all hope lost? Or could you entwine your string with itself in a way that approximates the surface you dream of? Good news: knitting’s got your back! And all you need to do is pull some loops through other loops. Knitted fabrics are breathable, flexible, and easy to construct either by hand or with a machine. They can stretch to about double their length without lengthening the constituent yarn. Knits are so popular that you are probably wearing one right now!

In this talk, we will learn how knitted textiles are constructed and explore topological models of knitting. We will learn what it means to be knittable and meet a new knitted stitch that physicists designed to be less prone to unraveling than standard knitting. You will also get to practice knitting a few stitches for yourself!

Susan Najita, University of Michigan

This paper explores the establishment of Hawai‘i Volcanoes National Park in the post-annexation period, two prominent newspaper serial publications of the saga of Pele, the goddess of the volcano, and her sister, Hi‘iaka, which reinvigorated connection to the place that would be brought under federal control. Her current project is entitled Genealogies of Place: Colonialism, Embodiment, and the Making of Hawai‘i Volcanoes National Park. 

Global Perspectives on Culture and Health explores fundamental aspects of human life. Culture facilitates human interaction by providing meaning to lived experience. Accounting for culture in both theories and methods potentially advances the study of health by connecting the macro and micro levels of human experience. Yet, culture should be understood as dynamic and complex. It fundamentally shapes individuals and simultaneously is shaped by individuals. The importance of systematically attending to culture includes topics of values, language, immigration, and society.

Theories and methods that incorporate culture hold great potential for advancing the understanding of health outcomes and health trajectories in various global contexts.

The speakers for this series will focus on various aspects of culture and diverse groups living in the U.S. and across the globe to address the ways in which attending to culture helps clarify and overcome challenges to good health.

event_title: Dynamics seminar: Boundary stratifications of Hurwitz spaces
combined_title: Dynamics seminar: Boundary stratifications of Hurwitz spaces: Darragh Glynn
description: A Hurwitz space is a moduli space parametrising holomorphic maps of Riemann surfaces with prescribed branching data. Building on work of Harris-Mumford, Abramovich-Corti-Vistoli describe a smooth compactification whose boundary parametrises degenerate maps. The boundary decomposes into connected subsets, or strata, corresponding to combinatorial types of degenerations. I will present recent results giving an explicit, implementable description of the strata. This description leads to a natural definition of a tropical Hurwitz space and has applications in complex dynamics.

description: We develop a new approach to estimating flexible demand models with exogenous supply-side shocks. event_title: GLNT: Arithmetic intersections on non-split Cartan modular curves
combined_title: GLNT: Arithmetic intersections on non-split Cartan modular curves: Jonathan Love (UM)
description: Abstract: Take two CM elliptic curves over a number field, each equipped with a level structure preserved by all endomorphisms. At which primes $p$ does there exist an isomorphism between the elliptic curves mod $p$ that preserves the level structures? This question was answered for $\Gamma_0(N)$ level structure by Gross, Kohnen, and Zagier in 1987. A key step in their proof is showing that an isomorphism mod $p$ determines embeddings of the (quadratic) CM orders into a common (quaternion) Eichler order. In this talk, we will discuss what changes in the argument when we replace $\Gamma_0(N)$ with the normalizer of a non-split Cartan subgroup. This is joint work with Elie Studnia and Jan Vonk.

event_title: ISRMT Seminar:  Many Body Asymptotics for the Toda Lattice
combined_title: ISRMT Seminar:  Many Body Asymptotics for the Toda Lattice: Amol Aggarwal (Stanford University)
description:
Abstract: The Toda lattice prescribes the evolution of many particles interacting under certain Hamiltonian dynamics; it is an archetypal example of a completely integrable system. In this talk we describe several results providing the long-time asymptotics of this system, under random, dense initial data. The proofs proceed by finding a way to interpret the Toda lattice as a collection of "quasi-particles" that behave similarly to solitons, and providing a framework to study how these quasi-particles asymptotically evolve in time. The arguments use ideas from random matrix theory, particularly the analysis localization phenomena for eigenvectors of random tridiagonal matrices.

Join Dr. Anand Parekh, Chief Health Policy Officer, School of Public Health and Senior Advisor, Institute for Healthcare Policy and Innovation, for this timely lecture on how health professionals can address social determinants of health. McKesson Foundation Health Equity Speaker Series
Disparities in health and healthcare have been are prevalent, particularly in underserved or minority communities, as a result of a variety of factors such as birthplace, housing, education, race, age, sexual identity and other nonmedical factors. These factors are commonly referred to as the social determinants of health (SDOH). As a result of SDOH, quality healthcare and treatment can be difficult to access for many who don’t fall into the dominant group and must confront barriers to receive treatment.

Examples of barriers to adequate healthcare treatment include poverty, lack of access to quality education or positive social activities, and unhealthy environmental factors. These factors must be addressed in order to achieve positive health outcomes and equity in access to healthcare and treatment for all. To help illuminate and educate around issues involving social determinants of health, the College of Pharmacy and the McKesson Foundation have teamed up to launch the McKesson Foundation Health Equity Speaker Series.

For the past two years the College of Pharmacy at the University of Michigan in partnership with the McKesson Foundation has hosted a speaker series based on the topic of health equity. The McKesson Foundation is dedicated to advancing health outcomes for all with the mission to removing barriers to quality healthcare across the country, especially for vulnerable and underserved communities. The College of Pharmacy also has a longstanding history of fighting to address addressing disparities in healthcare and is a leader in the fight for equitable healthcare for all individuals. This alignment in values and mission of both organizations led to the provision awarding of a grant to resulted in the College of Pharmacy being awarded a grant in 2022 to launch what we now call the McKesson Foundation Health Equity Speaker Series, with the goal of educating the UM community and inspiring those around us to find solutions that address inequities in healthcare and beyond.

About our Funder, the McKesson Foundation
The McKesson Foundation is a charitable organization dedicated to improving health outcomes for vulnerable and underserved populations. It focuses on initiatives that address healthcare disparities, promote patient-centered care, and support cancer care and survivorship. Through grants, partnerships, and employee-driven giving programs, the foundation aims to foster innovative solutions that enhance community health and well-being.

combined_title: Jia Yi Gu & Kate Yeh Chiu: Material Feasts | The Wallenberg Lecture
description:
Material Feast 
Material Feast is an interdisciplinary dialogue featuring designers and practitioners interrogating the contemporary role of materials in design. Framed as a “feast,” a term that gestures toward sensory abundance, the event invites us to consider materials as processes rather than products. Designers Brittanie Dabney, Catie Newell, Meredith Miller, Melanie McClintock, and Ana Morcillo Pallarés will each give a brief presentation of their practice, using provisional objects and material samples to probe the boundaries between art, science, design, and craft. Alongside the presentations, a material library will bring together samples drawn from automotive plastic waste streams, quagga mussels from lake systems, and waste glass, as well as perforated textiles, hydrogels, and brittle sponges made from foraged “kin” species.


Organized by Material Acts
Material Feast is organized by Material Acts (Kate Yeh Chiu, Jia Yi Gu and Hilary Huckins-Weidner), a research platform exploring materials as cultural technique through public events centering an experimental library. The project attends to the logistical, economic, and technological actions that transform matter into the material substrate for our lives. Initiated in 2021 as part of  Getty PST ART, the project has taken the form of a major exhibition at Craft Contemporary,  an editorial project with e-flux Architecture, and a publication of ideas, conversations, and material inquiries. Working through exhibitions, programming, and editorial projects, Material Acts brings together theoretical and practical engagements with materials, addressing how design and architecture are entangled with social and ecological concerns. www.materialacts.org

Contributors 

Brittanie Dabney
Brittanie Dabney is the founder and CEO of Ecosphere Organics, a Detroit-based company that converts food waste from local restaurants and suppliers into reusable materials. An environmental scientist trained at Wayne State University, she studied microplastic pollution, and her company now develops compostable packaging and plant-based leather alternatives at Newlab. She is adjunct faculty at the College for Creative Studies and served on the 2025 Detroit Month of Design curatorial committee.

Catie Newell
Catie Newell is Professor of Architecture at the University of Michigan's Taubman College, which she joined in 2009 as the Oberdick Fellow. She is the founding principal of Alibi Studio, established in Detroit in 2010, and her work explores materiality in relation to place through material systems, light, and darkness. She is a Lucas Fellow, a Kresge Artist Fellow, and a Fellow of the American Academy in Rome.

Meredith Miller
Meredith Miller is Associate Professor of Architecture and Director of the Master of Architecture program at Taubman College. She holds a BS from the University of Virginia and a Master of Architecture from Princeton. Amythyst Kiah: Presented by The Ark
description:
“One of Americana’s great up-and-coming secrets.” –Rolling Stone

On her new album Still + Bright, Tennessee-bred singer/songwriter Amythyst Kiah explores the vast expanse of her inner world: her deep-rooted affinity for Eastern philosophies and spiritual traditions, a near-mystical connection with the natural environment, the life lessons learned in her formative years as a self-described “anime-nerd mall goth,” and much more. Produced by Butch Walker (Taylor Swift, Green Day, Weezer) and recorded at his Nashville studio, Kiah’s second full-length for Rounder Records merges her revelatory storytelling with a darkly cinematic twist on the rootsy alt-rock of her 2021 breakthrough Wary + Strange—an LP that landed on Rolling Stone’s list of the 25 Best Country and Americana Albums of 2021 and drew acclaim from major outlets like Pitchfork. With its sonic palette encompassing everything from fuzzed-out guitars and industrial-leaning beats to gilded pedal steel and Kiah’s exquisitely graceful banjo work, Still + Bright makes for a vital new addition to a body of work largely dedicated to exploring the struggle and joy of true self-discovery.

The latest turn in a dynamic career that’s included joining Our Native Daughters (an all-women-of-color supergroup also featuring Rhiannon Giddens, Leyla McCalla, and Allison Russell), Still + Bright emerged from a deliberate transformation of the songwriting process Kiah adopted after composing her first song on a Fender acoustic at age 13. To that end, the album marks her first time opening up her approach and working with co-writers, including punk legend Tim Armstrong, Sadler Vaden (a guitarist/vocalist for Jason Isbell’s 400 Unit), and former Pentatonix member Avi Kaplan. Although her third LP is an undeniable departure from the anguished emotionality of its predecessor (an album informed by losing her mother to suicide at age 17), Kiah imparts each track with a hypnotic intensity born from boldly stating her convictions. Revealing her rare ability to spin her fascinations into songs uncovering essential truths about human nature, Still + Bright ultimately affirms her as an artist of both daring originality and uncompromising depth.

Lila Kadaj received her MFA from Wayne State University. Her work has been shown at numerous institutions, including the Detroit Institute of Arts, the Cranbrook Art Museum, and the Arab American National Museum.  She spent nearly 27 years teaching art at Detroit Public schools.

Artist statement: “When looking at a beautiful flower.  It’s just itself.  Just there......no .....it does not proclaim its purpose for blooming is to make people happy. It just is. Like standing in front of an easel and painting........just is.......no matter......what proclamations may be concluded to sway the viewer. Same thing goes for fine art.  It’s not about I am a woman....it’s not about I am a first generation Arab American.....it’s not about being a child of trauma....it’s not about a member of my family being gunned down on the street....it’s about being born a painter.....standing in front of my easel and working to create a "Piece of Fine Art". Not standing on some soap box and expecting my words to somehow qualify my painting. It’s the painting, drawing or sculpture that must speak on its own.......on how the artist......via the intellect and muse uses the elements to create something distinct and first rate.   It can be quiet or loud. I see so much very weak work uplifted not for its quality but because it’s in fashion.”

event_title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
combined_title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
description:
Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union.

Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky  portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration.  

“For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.”
— Galina Lembersky, daughter

Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director.

combined_title: Black Birth Joy: Announcing Lane Hall’s Fall Exhibition
description:
Black Birth Joy by Tiana Lashae documents birth as a deeply personal story of connection, courage, tenderness, and joy. The photographs and stories in the exhibit challenge mainstream narratives that reduce Black birth to statistics and only amplify Black pregnant women's anxiety and hesitancy about navigating the maternal health care system. Instead, the exhibit offers evidence of joy, reminders of possibility, and a visual legacy for generations to come. 
 
Black Birth Joy was born from Lashae's belief that more positive birth stories of BIPOC families need to be seen and heard, and her photographs invite viewers to witness the people behind them: the mothers, babies, partners, families, and birthworkers. They create space for BIPOC families to see themselves represented with dignity and to witness the full range of birth experiences. Lashae's photographs also create a tangible record that can support conversations around quality of medical care, respectful treatment, and patient rights. The exhibit empowers women to prioritize and advocate for their birth experiences while also encouraging perinatal health professionals and birthworkers to center the humanity, dignity, and individual experiences of patients and families. 

The exhibit comprises over 30 photographs as well as stories of mothers whose births were documented by Lashae, a doula and birth/newborn photographer whose work has been published in Everyday Birth Magazine, an international publication. The physical exhibit is accompanied by a virtual component that encourages audiences to engage with each mother's birth story.

The Lane Hall Exhibit Space is sponsored by the Institute for Research on Women and Gender (IRWG) and the Department of Women’s and Gender Studies (WGS) at the University of Michigan.

description:
Visit the Hatcher Gallery Exhibit Room to see historical materials that illustrate women’s changing relationship with food, cooking, and technology during the heady decade of the 1920s, sandwiched between WWI and the Great Depression. This exhibit features materials from the Janice Bluestein Longone Culinary Archive, as well as select items from the Art, Architecture, and Engineering Special Collections and the Transportation History Collection.

As America rang in a new decade in the 1920s, cookbook authors and appliance manufacturers stood ready to offer the newly emancipated and forward-thinking American woman a vision for her future, a vision that would be scientifically  grounded, speedy enough to make time for leisure as well as housework, and guaranteed to bring fun to that most humdrum of chores: planning and preparing meals for a family three times a day, 365 days a year.

combined_title: Like the flowing river: An exhibition by Tomoyuki Ueno
description:
Artist Tomoyuki Ueno creates individual works and installations where nature appears to be in an endless conversation with form, one echoing the other, a repetition. They are a combination of certainty and ephemerality, as if hinged between living and loss. The specificity of Ueno’s sculptural works reads like poetry. Ueno’s installation offers visitors time away, for contemplation, to draw inward, to come inside, to ask the question, “How are art and the everyday intertwined?” Honoring the Buddhist philosophy of impermanence, one becomes a continuation of the other. The artist intends the space to offer a restorative and meditative experience.

This exhibition includes artworks created from natural materials foraged by the artist while in artist residency in Ann Arbor.

*The title refers to the opening line of Hōjōki, written by 13th-century Japanese Buddhist monk Kamo no Chōmei: "The flow of the river is ceaseless, and the water is never the same…"*

Small Works was a print shop ran by Li Chen & Gerald Schulze, in Detroit, MI, from 2020–2026. Mariana Matos joined as the studio assistant, and later studio manager, in 2024. Over those six years, the business grew from an extension of their design practice to a community space that hosts more than 70 classes a year, open studio for the public, and year long funded fellowships that investigate practice in art and design related to the Book Arts. In 2026, they decided to expand community programming, and to accommodate this expansion closed Small Works, and formed Center for the Book Arts Detroit (BAD) which operates in the same space.

This exhibition is a eulogy for the former Small Works shop, and a celebration of all the people who made work here. It also serves to show what is possible as a community, when they share space and create work together. 

The work featured is a collection of things printed by Small Works, by their studiomates Diskette Press, the publisher Maamoul Press, and by the community that uses the space.

description:
The lifelike naturalistic bodies of Greek and Roman sculpture have been a source of wonder since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Italian Renaissance artist Vasari identified the ancient world as the time “when sculpture rose to its greatest height.” But close likenesses of the natural world are not the only visual products of the ancient past. This exhibition traces alternative visual trends in the ancient Roman world that today would be considered examples of abstraction. It focuses on monuments and motifs long pushed to the margins of our accounts of ancient art. Oversize arrangements of interlocking shapes pulsate in bold block colors from tombs, temples, and homes; stylized animals flicker into view, only to collapse once more into bright geometric arrangements; and artists adopt experimental shorthands for the depiction of space across media. Anticipating recent interests in color and form, the visual trends of antiquity emerge as far more varied than has long been told.

*Ancient Abstractions is on view from November 5, 2026, through February 28, 2027, during regular museum hours (Tuesday–Friday, 10:00 AM–4:00 PM, and Saturday–Sunday, 11:00 AM–4:00 PM; closed Mondays and university holidays.*

event_title: From Code to Composition: Personalized Recommendations and Product Innovation (joint with Maria Trejos, Diana Van Patten, and Kai Hao)
combined_title: From Code to Composition: Personalized Recommendations and Product Innovation (joint with Maria Trejos, Diana Van Patten, and Kai Hao): David Argente, Yale University
description: This paper studies how personalized recommendation algorithms (PRAs), a central application of artificial intelligence, shape product innovation. We develop an equilibrium model in which consumers have heterogeneous tastes, producers choose product characteristics subject to costs, and a platform recommends products while learning preferences from noisy signals. Personalization changes producers' incentives by allowing them to target different consumer segments. This response can increase market-wide differentiation and make new products more distinct from the existing stock, even when personalization narrows individual exposure. We examine these implications in the music industry, where PRAs have been widely adopted since the mid-2010s. Using tools from music information retrieval applied to raw audio files, we find that songs have become more original, both within a given year and relative to past releases, following the widespread adoption of PRAs. We extend the model to CES preferences and combine our originality estimates with listening-time shares to quantify the welfare implications. The implied consumer-surplus gains associated with additional originality range from 2.2% to 2.4% in 2023 relative to a counterfactual with originality fixed at its 2013 level.

event_title: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”
combined_title: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”
description:
Changes over the course of the nineteenth century in how Americans voted, from voice vote to public ballot box to private voting booth, also saw changes in the material culture that surrounded voting. Ballots and ballot boxes, campaign pins and ribbons, blank lists and pre-printed party tickets, lanterns and banners–the creative forces of the American print industry filled the country’s cities and small towns with the ephemera of electioneering.

As you look at the items in this exhibit, think about what they tell us about how Americans in the past felt about voting, and about how voting felt. How did Election Days feel when they were full of parades and music and public drinking? What was it like to vote when everyone around you knew who you voted for? And, most of all, who counted as a voter, and who did the counting?

On view September 11-December 22, weekdays from 12-4 pm.

event_title: Cosmo Whyte: Under the Quiet, Beyond the Eye
combined_title: Cosmo Whyte: Under the Quiet, Beyond the Eye
description:
Curated by Srimoyee Mitra

Stamps Gallery kicks off the fall 2026 semester with an ambitious mid-career survey of interdisciplinary artist Cosmo Whyte. Born and raised in Jamaica, Whyte completed a BFA from Bennington College and earned an MFA from the University of Michigan. He is currently a faculty member at the School of the Arts and Architecture, UCLA.

This exhibition brings together two central concerns that animate Whyte’s artistic practice: the archive, both personal and public, as a site of disturbance; and migration as a lived experience of refuge, refusal, and reinvention. In Whyte’s work, the archive is never static or neutral. Rather, it is a contested space where official histories encounter memory, inheritance, and the fragments of stories carried across generations. His practice moves within this charged interstitial terrain, between what has been recorded and what has been remembered, between institutional knowledge and embodied experience. Whyte invites the viewer to consider the fluidity of geographic borders and layered cultural identities that have persisted despite societal unrest caused by racial and socio-economic hierarchies across generations. In an era of intensified border politics and renewed debates over national identity, Whyte’s work offers a timely meditation on memory, movement, and belonging.

Presented with support from the U-M Institute for Humanities, the U-M LSA Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies, and the U-M Library.

description:
Negative emotions at work are inevitable, but they don’t have to derail your performance or well-being. Many of us default to hiding or ignoring difficult feelings; without the right tools, that can lead to unintended consequences and missed insight.

Advancing the Human Health and Well-Being impact area of U-M’s Look to Michigan vision, this global virtual panel will explore how mental fitness supports career growth. Ethan Kross, renowned U-M professor, international bestselling author of Chatter and Shift, and director of the U-M Mental Fitness Institute — a moonshot effort to reduce global suffering — will be joined by career coach Stacy Kim, author of Envy, to share practical strategies for managing and using negative emotions more effectively.

Using envy as a case study, they’ll show how emotions can reveal what you want, what to pursue, and who to learn from.

Myths we’ll challenge: 

There are “good” and “bad” emotions
Avoidance is always toxic, and venting is always helpful
Comparing yourself with others is the problem

You’ll leave with:

Concrete tools and exercises to build mental fitness at work  
Strategies for handling emotional “chatter” and relationship curveballs  
Greater calm, confidence, and clarity; plus resources to learn more

combined_title: LRCCS Noon Lecture Series | Chinese and Muslim Refugees on the Tibetan Frontier, 1860–1965: Gyatso Marnyi, University of Michigan
description:
From 1860 onward, frequent wars and disasters claimed millions of lives in Northwest China. More than one million Chinese and Muslims sought refuge on the northeastern Tibetan Plateau. This talk explores the diverse experiences of these refugees as they crossed multiple ethnocultural and administrative boundaries, lived
alongside Tibetans, and forged new homelands during China’s transition from empire to nation-state.

Gyatso Marnyi is a historian of empires and frontiers in Asia. Combining textual sources with ethnographic fieldwork, his research examines interactions and exchanges between China and surrounding Asian regions from the fourteenth to the twentieth century. He is currently completing a monograph that explores the uneven
experiences of Tibetan, Mongol, Chinese, and Muslim communities during China’s transition from empire to nation-state on the Inner Asian frontier.

combined_title: The Tree of Eternity: Interactive arttech exhibit
description:
The Tree of Eternity is an immersive, interactive installation that explores remembrance, loss, and the enduring presence of those we have loved. 

The installation centers on a projected tree surrounded by interactive terminal pods that control its structure.

Visitors approach interactive pods positioned throughout the gallery space, where they are invited to recall memories of people or experiences throughout their lives. Depending on the kiosk they interact with, different effects will be present on the projected tree.

As more visitors’ memories are inputted, the tree’s visuals adapt and change form, demonstrating that our memories persist with us. Projection mapping creates ethereal visuals accompanied by atmospheric audio. Even when visitors aren't actively engaging with the kiosks, the system generates ambient transmissions, suggesting that the tree—and the memories it embodies—continues to live and grow.

The installation creates a dialogue between life and death, presence and absence, individual memory and collective remembrance, inviting participants to contribute to a living memorial that persists beyond any single moment of grief or reflection.

University Carillonist Tiffany Ng performs on the Charles Baird Carillon, an instrument of 53 bronze bells located inside the Burton Memorial Tower. The largest bell, which strikes the hour, weighs 12 tons, while the smallest bell, 4½ octaves above, weighs just 15 pounds.

Thirty-minute recitals are performed on the Charles Baird Carillon at noon every weekday that classes are in session, followed by visitor Q&A with the carillonist. The bell chamber may be accessed via a combination of elevator and stairs. Take the elevator to the highest floor possible (floor 8), and then climb two flights of stairs (39 steps) to the bell chamber (floor 10). Hearing protection earmuffs are provided for visitors. Be prepared to walk on ice and snow in the bell chamber during winter. Built in 1936, the Charles Baird Carillon is not ADA accessible. Visitors with mobility concerns are invited to visit the Lurie Carillon.

event_title: Radical Care: Women, Antifascism, and Archival Silences in the Spanish Civil War
combined_title: Radical Care: Women, Antifascism, and Archival Silences in the Spanish Civil War: A Hear, Here: Humanities Up Close event with Anna Müller
event_subtitle: A Hear, Here: Humanities Up Close event with Anna Müller
description:
With the “Hear, Here” series, we aim to facilitate conversations around new research in the humanities. Faculty fellows at the Institute for the Humanities will discuss a part of their current project in a short talk followed by a Q & A session.

About this talk:
What can we know about women who crossed borders to fight fascism when their surviving stories were recorded largely by institutions that scrutinized their loyalty? This talk follows women volunteers from Poland, many of them Jewish migrants, whose work as part of the International Brigades, in the Spanish Civil War, turned care into a form of political commitment. Reading questionnaires, political assessments, letters, and photographs, it explores how communist organizations enabled women’s participation while subjecting them to gendered suspicion and unstable classifications of nationality and belonging. These fragmentary lives raise broader questions about how historians interpret archival silences, recover possibilities obscured by bureaucratic judgments, and write responsibly about experiences they cannot fully reconstruct.

Anna Müller is a 2026–27 Norman Freehling Visiting Faculty Fellow at the Institute for the Humanities and Professor of History and Polish/Polish American/Eastern European Studies at U-M Dearborn.

combined_title: AI Futures Keynote: Julie Schell: Taking Teaching with AI Seriously: Socratic Tutors as AI Pedagogy
event_subtitle: Taking Teaching with AI Seriously: Socratic Tutors as AI Pedagogy
description:
What happens when faculty move beyond debating AI’s role in education and begin designing, testing, and evaluating new approaches in their own courses – all without a playbook?

Schell will share case studies of faculty across disciplines who are building AI pedagogy from the ground up using Socratic AI tutors. Through examples of tutor prompts and instructions, she will show the pedagogical challenges faculty set out to address, the choices they made in designing their tutors, and what they learned from using them with students.

Drawing on a year of student–tutor interactions, she will also examine evidence of how students use faculty-built AI tutors to practice behaviors that can be difficult to foster and observe, including metacognition, error processing, and self-directed learning. The findings suggest a compelling possibility: Thoughtfully designed AI may create new opportunities for students to practice the difficult thinking that meaningful learning requires.


*About AI Futures Keynote Speaker Series*
The Center for Academic Innovation is convening leading voices in academia to examine emerging applications of artificial intelligence in higher education. The AI Futures keynote speaker series is a critical examination of how artificial intelligence is reshaping teaching and learning as we consider the future of life changing education at Michigan.

event_title: Local Asymptotics for Treatment Choice with Partial Identification
combined_title: Local Asymptotics for Treatment Choice with Partial Identification: Jörg Stoye, Cornell University
description: We provide a new asymptotic framework to derive approximately optimal treatment assignments when sampling noise from data is compounded by fundamental uncertainty due to partial identification. We recenter the reduced-form parameter around its \emph{least-favorable} configuration and consider drifting parameter sequences that yield both diminishing levels of sampling uncertainty and of partial identification. We characterize the limiting decision problem as a normal location shift model with a suitable limiting identified set. We apply our results to treatment choice problems with contaminated outcomes, to robust welfare analyses with partially identified consumer surplus, and to the problem of aggregating experimental estimates for policy adoption.

Learn how to ignite the science of extraordinary organizations catalyzed by human thriving, together with our community of researchers, students, staff, and leaders.

About the talk:
Why is it so hard to speak up, even when we know something’s wrong? 

Many of us comply much more than we realize. How many times have you wanted to object, disagree, or opt out of something—but ended up swallowing your words, shaking your head, and just going along? Discussing the ideas and frameworks from her bestselling book *DEFY*, Dr. Sunita Sah will delve into why the pressure to comply is a corrosive and often invisible force in our society, and what we can do about it. 

Drawing on her original research on compliance, defiance, insinuation anxiety, and voice, you’ll learn to:

+Show+ up authentically in personal and professional situations
+Understand+ the difference between defiance, compliance, and consent
+Practice+ defiance in low-stakes scenarios to build confidence
+Recognize+ your body’s warning signals that it’s time to act
+Navigate+ workplace pressure without losing your integrity (or your job)

Defiance isn’t about being loud or combative. It’s about acting in alignment with your values, even when it’s hard. *DEFY* will show you how to do it every day, in every part of your life

About Sah:
Dr. Sunita Sah is the National bestselling author of *DEFY*, an award-winning professor at Cornell University, and an expert in organizational psychology. She leads groundbreaking research on influence, authority, trust, compliance, and defiance. A trained physician, she practiced medicine in the United Kingdom and worked as a management consultant for the pharmaceutical industry. Abstract
Adolescence is a time of identity formation, when young people figure out who they are and who they want to be. One of the ways they do this is by considering the world around them, paying attention to social issues and starting to understand their society and their place in it. Laws and policies signal to young people what society thinks of their value, their role in society and their opportunities for the future. But the experience of growing up in the post-Roe v. Wade era looks very different from that before the 50-year precedent was overturned in 2022. Following the Dobbs v. Jackson Supreme Court decision, two-thirds of U.S. adolescents now live in a state with severely restricted or no legal abortion access. As a result, today’s young people are coming of age in what has been termed an “era of rights retractions.” This talk will provide a data-based account of how, following Dobbs, the experience of adolescence and young adulthood in America has fundamentally changed and how rights retractions are not only affecting those who need an abortion – they are shaping an entire generation.

Biography:
Dr. Julie Maslowsky is Associate Professor of Health Behavior and Clinical Sciences at the University of Michigan School of Nursing, Associate Professor of Health Behavior and Health Equity at the University of Michigan School of Public Health, and Research Associate Professor at the UM Institute for Social Research.  She is a developmental psychologist and population health scientist who studies adolescent health, with a focus on sexual and reproductive health including contraception and abortion. Her research integrates adolescent developmental science with population and reproductive health to inform developmentally appropriate policies and practices on adolescent sexual and reproductive health.

event_title: MICDE State of AI: End-to-End Computational Scientific Discovery
combined_title: MICDE State of AI: End-to-End Computational Scientific Discovery: Speakers: Kai Sun, Professor of Physics and Venkat Viswanathan, Professor of Aerospace Engineering
event_subtitle: Speakers: Kai Sun, Professor of Physics and Venkat Viswanathan, Professor of Aerospace Engineering
description: This special event will present a recent breakthrough by professors Kai Sun (Physics) and Venkat Viswanathan (Aerospace). Fractional Chern insulators are exotic topological states of matter that host anyons, a proposed foundation for fault-tolerant quantum computing, but their small energy gaps confine them to extremely low temperatures. The team asked frontier AI models to propose a new theoretical framework for topological flat bands, then set a swarm of agents to explore it, coordinating only through a shared message board, with every candidate checked by GPU-accelerated exact diagonalization. The swarm found a surprise: departing from the “ideal” quantum geometry long considered optimal raised the many-body gap more than tenfold over the starting bands, well past the previous benchmark and beyond what agents working alone reached. AI-assisted analysis then distilled this into a simple sheared Landau level model that explains the mechanism (reshaped electron orbitals stiffen the short-range repulsion protecting the state) and yields a design index computable without many-body simulation. Proposing the hypothesis, searching it,  explaining what it found, and presenting a model offers an early look at end-to-end scientific discovery with AI.

event_title: CM-AMO Seminar | Computing and Networking with Neutral-Atom Quantum Processors
combined_title: CM-AMO Seminar | Computing and Networking with Neutral-Atom Quantum Processors: Kevin Singh (Ohio State University)
description: Neutral-atom arrays have emerged as a promising platform for scalable quantum information processing, combining long-lived qubits, programmable Rydberg interactions, and natural interconnection with photonic qubits. In this talk, I will discuss our efforts to develop new architectures that address key challenges in scaling neutral-atom processors toward fault-tolerant quantum computation and distributed quantum networks. I will first describe a dual-isotope rubidium architecture that provides isotope-selective control while retaining nearly identical Rydberg-Rydberg resonances, thereby enabling new approaches to mid-circuit measurement, qubit addressing, and high-fidelity entangling gates. I will then discuss our development of photonically integrated neutral-atom processors based on ytterbium atoms coupled to fiber Fabry–Perot cavities. These photonic interfaces aim to efficiently connect atomic qubits to telecom photons, providing a pathway toward long-distance quantum networks and distributed quantum computing. I will then discuss our efforts to build a large-scale quantum internet in Ohio.

description:
Robotics Department Seminar Series (https://robotics.umich.edu/events/robotics-seminar-series/)
Speaker: Wanzek Family Foundation Collegiate Professor of Engineering; Associate Professor in Aerospace and Mechanical Engineering, University of Notre Dame
Title: "What Scale Won’t Buy: Physical Structure for Robots in an Era of Data"
Date: Tuesday, November 17, 2026

Location: FRB 2300 + Zoom
Zoom Link: https://myumi.ch/AxG9Z
Meeting ID: 997 8617 1873

Abstract: Robot learning is in a period of extraordinary momentum. Humanoids now learn athletic, whole-body skills from simulation and human demonstration, while industry investment accelerates the push toward general-purpose machines. Much of this progress relies on synthetic or retargeted data and inherits whatever physics those pipelines get right or wrong. More data alone is not enough. Robots also need models that respect physics, demonstrations they can physically execute, and interfaces that let them work intuitively with people. This talk argues that physical structure is not a competitor to learning but part of its infrastructure.

I will first discuss differentiable simulation and data pipelines for the closed-chain mechanisms of real humanoids, along with physically consistent model identification grounded in the geometry of mass distributions. I will then present dynamics-aware retargeting and whole-body MPC that turn human motion into feasible robot behavior, including heavy-payload loco-manipulation where vision alone cannot determine payload dynamics. This emphasis on structure also extends to machines that must coordinate with the human body. In lower-limb prostheses, I will show how task-level priors drawn from human sensorimotor coordination allow humanlike joint behavior to emerge from whole-body coordination rather than being prescribed joint by joint. Across robots and people alike, scale makes good structure more valuable, not less.

Speaker Bio: Patrick Wensing is the Wanzek Family Foundation Collegiate Professor of Engineering and an Associate Professor in Aerospace and Mechanical Engineering at the University of Notre Dame, where he directs the Robotics, Optimization, and Assistive Mobility (ROAM) Lab. He received his Ph.D. in Electrical and Computer Engineering from The Ohio State University in 2014 and completed postdoctoral training at MIT in 2017, where he worked on control system design for the MIT Cheetah robots. His research focuses on dynamics, optimization, and control to advance the mobility of legged robots and assistive devices. Dr. Wensing is a recipient of the NSF CAREER Award (2020) and the IROS Toshio Fukuda Young Professional Award (2023), and his work has been recognized with multiple best paper awards. He currently serves as an Editor for the IEEE Transactions on Robotics and as a member of the IEEE RAS Executive Committee.

event_title: U-M History Film Series: Ten Times Better + About Face
combined_title: U-M History Film Series: Ten Times Better + About Face: Jennifer Lin (Director)
description:
Join the History Department on the evening of Tuesday, November 17, for a screening of two documentary shorts, Ten Times Better (2024) and About Face (2025), followed by a conversation with director Jennifer Lin. This event will take place in the Screening Room at the Michigan Theater starting at 5:30 pm.

Following each film, there will be a panel discussion with Lin, moderated by Ian Shin (History) and Fangfei Miao (Dance). 

Ten Times Better - Runtime 30m

From ballet to Broadway to blackjack, George Lee of Las Vegas has seen it all in his 89 years, but never had his moment to shine. Until now. This short documentary elevates George’s contribution to dance, including originating the Chinese role in George Balanchine’s The Nutcracker and working with director Gene Kelly in Flower Drum Song. Plans are underway for a national PBS broadcast of the film, which has been featured in the New York Times and AARP magazine.

About Face - Runtime 1hr

This feature-length documentary spotlights Phil Chan and Georgina Pazcoguin, two NYC dancers of Asian descent who founded the Final Bow for Yellowface movement to  jettison offensive Asian stereotypes, including dancing in yellowface, from classical ballet. The pair is taking on entrenched tradition and political pushback as they shine a critical spotlight on The Nutcracker and other beloved classics like La Bayadere in this vivid account of cultural missteps and creative evolution.

Jennifer Lin is a veteran journalist, who was stationed in Beijing, New York and Washington, D.C. for The Philadelphia Inquirer. Beyond Yellowface is her third film project. In 2013, she produced Geil of Doylestown: Forgotten Explorer. In 2021, she produced and co-directed Beethoven in Beijing, which premiered nationally on PBS’s Great Performances and was a finalist for the Library of Congress Lavine/Ken Burns Prize for Film. 

Fangfei Miao, an international dance theorist, choreographer, and dancer, is Assistant Professor of Dance in the School of Music, Theatre, & Dance at the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, where she teaches both seminar and physical practice courses. Miao’s scholarly research weaves dance and performance studies, Chinese and East Asian studies, and critical inquiries into globalization. Her in-progress monograph examines the productive historical “mis-steps” engendered by Sino-US cross-cultural dance transmissions in Reform-Era China (1978-the present).

Ian Shin is a social and cultural historian of the United States and Associate Professor of History and American Culture. His research and teaching focus on Asian American history and on the history of the U.S. in the Pacific World between 1850 and 1950. Shin comes to this work as a first-generation American who was born in Hong Kong, grew up in California, and spent the past decade and a half on the East Coast. His work is guided not only by his training in historical methods but also by my dedication to critical race and ethnic studies. He is the author of Imperial Stewards: Chinese Art and the Making of America's Pacific Century (Stanford University Press, 2025).

This event is free and open to the public.

event_title: Wind, Light, and the Moment of Death
combined_title: Wind, Light, and the Moment of Death: by Lee von Kraus, PhD
description:
Doctors and nurses sometimes observe surprising phenomena at a patient's time of death, including sudden gusts of wind, electrical malfunctions, and even floating lights. While these "perimortem observations" (PMOs) have fascinating implications, further research has been limited by ethical and methodological barriers.

Join Dr. Lee von Kraus, a pioneer in the study of perimortem observations, in a discussion of recent research that suggests PMOs are not hallucinations or coincidences, but are instead death-correlated, mechanically obscure physical phenomena.

Presented by: Lee von Kraus, PhD, Chief Scientist, Open Minded Scientists

description:
All screenings will be held in Space2435 North Quad. Movies will be shown in Italian with English subtitles. Free and open to the public. 

Tuesday September 29th @ 7:00 PM 
*Il Sorpasso *
On a deserted Ferragosto in Rome, a shy young law student is drawn into a spontaneous road trip by a brash, fast-talking stranger with a sports car. As the two men speed along the coast, their comic misadventures reveal the pleasures and anxieties of Italy’s economic boom. In Italian with English subtitles. Directed by Dino Risi,1962.

Tuesday October 27th @ 7:00 PM 
*La Signora senza camelie*
It’s the story of a shopclerk named Clara who finds a chance casting in a small movie role develop into a full-blown career as screen-siren. Tension erupts when her husband can no longer tolerate watching her frivolous cinema escapades, and pushes her into a “serious, artistic” production of the life of Joan of Arc… whereupon she is castigated by the critical establishment. Featuring Lucia Bose, Gino Cervi, Alain Cuny. In Italian with English subtitles. Directed by Michelangelo Antonioni, 1953.

Tuesday November 17th @ 7:00 PM
*Catene *
In the first of a series of meladramas directed by Matarazzo, a husband kills his wife's ex-boyfriend, who was blackmailing her. He flees to America, but is sent back to Italy to stand trial. The only way he can be set free is if his wife confesses to adultery—so the murder can be considered a crime of passion—but this estranges her from her family. In Italian with English subtitles. Directed by Raffaello Matarazzo, 1949.

The Great Lakes Writers Corps is a unique and generously funded experiential 3-part sequence (winter, summer, fall) offered by the University of Michigan English Department. Over the course of the program, which consists of two courses bookending an independent summer field work project, GLWC students learn how to research and compose purposeful, long-form journalistic stories on topics centering the experience of Great Lakes communities. Students will develop their own takes on these topics through immersive investigation of the region’s geography, ecosystems, cultural history, politics, and/or connection to the concept of home.
